priority: terminal/peduncled versus axillary/nearly sessile flower position
long-pilose versus fine short pubescence versus nearly glabrous foliage
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify these from purple flower color alone. Flower position and hair type are the fastest field split.

quick_key.if: purple/violet flowers raised above the foliage on conspicuous peduncled branching terminal or upper-axillary cymes; foliage mostly glabrous to inconspicuously hairy
quick_key.then: Ruellia ciliatiflora (= R. nudiflora / R. occidentalis source concepts)

quick_key.if: purple flowers/cymes essentially sessile in the leaf axils; stems and leaves finely short-pubescent; capsule with only 2–4 seeds
purple flowers nearly sessile in leaf axils AND stems/leaves/margins conspicuously long-pilose or shaggy
large white to pale flowers in a terminal branching panicle; upper inflorescence and calyx densely stalked-glandular-hairy

taxonomy_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Ruellia ciliatiflora Hook. and places Ruellia nudiflora and Ruellia occidentalis in synonymy. The project keeps historical Texas source names as aliases while using one canonical R. ciliatiflora learner.

look_here_first: 1) Find where each FLOWER STALK begins. Is the plant carrying a raised terminal/upper-axillary branching CYME (R. ciliatiflora, R. metziae), or are flowers clustered ALMOST SESSILE at a foliage leaf AXIL (R. drummondiana, R. humilis)? 2) Compare actual HAIR LENGTH on stem and leaf margins at the same scale: conspicuously LONG PILOSE/CILIATE R. humilis, versus fine SHORT PUBESCENCE of R. drummondiana. 3) On terminal-flowered plants, check white to pale flowers and conspicuously STALKED GLANDULAR HAIRS on the metziae calyx/inflorescence versus typically violet ciliatiflora. 4) When fruiting, compare SEED COUNT and opened CAPSULE RETINACULA; a true macro is needed. DO NOT use purple color alone.
shared_traits: Simple opposite leaves often DECUSSATE (successive leaf pairs rotated about 90 degrees). Stems often somewhat four-angled at least when young; these characters are shared with several unrelated families.
Five-lobed corollas arise from a funnel-shaped corolla tube; flowers may be white, violet or purple and are not reliably separated by color alone.
Some Ruellia bloom from raised terminal/peduncled branching cymes; others flower on short almost sessile axillary branches. This POSITION is the genus's best first species split.
Fruit matures as a dry capsule, typically 2-locular with hinged seed-support RETINACULA/JACULATORS. The family character needs a verified macro; current gallery pictures mostly show flowering shoots.
Stalked glandular hairs on the calyx/upper flowers and ordinary long ciliate leaf-edge hairs are different plant structures, and both are highly useful for distinguishing species.

overlap_cautions: R. ciliatiflora and R. metziae both carry raised terminal/upper-axillary clusters; use stalked calyx/inflorescence glands and floral details rather than corolla color alone.
R. humilis and R. drummondiana both have axillary nearly sessile flowers; compare actual hair length on matching stem/leaf positions and mature capsule seed number.
Flower color is not an independent diagnosis; lighting, age, and pale morphs can mislead.
R. nudiflora, R. occidentalis and R. nudiflora var. nudiflora are represented source concepts under canonical R. ciliatiflora, not extra species.
realistic_lookalikes: Ruellia simplex — long, narrow lanceolate leaves and a typically taller habit; a landscape escape that requires structural confirmation
Justicia species — bilabiate flowers and different capsule/inflorescence architecture
Dyschoriste linearis — smaller axillary flowers, narrow foliage, and distinct calyx/capsule morphology

matched leaf-axil flower attachment: R. drummondiana and R. humilis

lateral calyx and upper peduncle macros with scale: R. metziae vs R. ciliatiflora

genus_diagnostics.flower_position: An AXIL is the angle where a LEAF meets the STEM. 'SESSILE' (or nearly sessile) flowers have almost no obvious elongated supporting stalk. A PEDUNCLE is the stalk of a flower cluster (CYME); a PEDICEL supports one individual flower. Long branching terminal/upper-axillary clusters suggest R. ciliatiflora or metziae. Short nearly stalkless leaf-axil clusters suggest R. humilis or drummondiana. Follow the branch to its origin before deciding.
genus_diagnostics.leaf_hairs: PUBESCENCE means plant hairs. PILOSE describes comparatively long soft hairs; CILIATE means a conspicuous fringe of hairs ON THE LEAF EDGE. Humilis has many visibly long hairs especially on leaf margins; drummondiana tends to short/fine hairs; ciliatiflora can be very sparse or inconspicuously short-hairy. Same magnification and stem position are necessary.
genus_diagnostics.glandular_hairs: A GLANDULAR HAIR is a hair with a minute swollen secretory tip; stalked glands are distinctive on the calyx lobes and upper flowering branches of R. metziae. Simple hairs and stalked glands can coexist; do not label an ordinary hair a gland unless the head is in focus.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Leaves are SIMPLE and generally OPPOSITE/DECUSSATE (successive pairs at right angles); two leaf stalks may form slight ridges at a node. Compare complete ovate to elliptic blades, leaf margin and hairiness, but avoid calling species from shape alone.
genus_diagnostics.corolla: The COROLLA is the joined petal structure: a narrow TUBE widens to a funnel/throat with five free-ended LOBES. A flower can be violet, pale lavender or white; metziae often bright white. Do not infer the sex, seed count or gland density from flower color.
genus_diagnostics.calyx: The CALYX is the green outer ring of five narrow SEPAL lobes below the corolla. Fine hairs/gland-tipped hairs on calyx lobes offer strong Ruellia comparisons, especially metziae versus ciliatiflora. Need macro shots with specimen provenance and precise arrows.
genus_diagnostics.stamens: Ruellia commonly has FOUR fertile STAMENS in two length pairs attached to the inner flower tube (didynamous), not the two visible exserted stamens of certain Justicia-like relatives. They are often not visible from a distant front photo. Dissection macro needed before pointing to precise filament/anther pairs.
genus_diagnostics.capsule: The elongate dry, often 2-chambered CAPSULE opens in two longitudinal VALVES; hooked seed-supports (RETINACULA or JACULATORS) help flick seeds away. R. drummondiana has exceptionally few seeds (roughly 2–4 in the local treatment), while humilis typically bears more. Open a RIPE capsule to count, not a green bud. Don't imply the current flower portraits show retinacula.
genus_diagnostics.stem: Four-sided young stems and opposite leaves help route to Acanthaceae but neither is genus-exclusive. Look at the leaf nodes and the upper inflorescence for more decisive species characters.

comparison_cards.title: Humilis vs drummondiana — hairy vs fuzzy
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both have flowers almost SESSILE in the leaf AXILS. Humilis shows LONG individual PILOSE stem hairs and a CILIATE fringe along the leaf margin. Drummondiana usually has a finer SHORT fuzzy pubescence. In a fruiting plant inspect mature capsule seed number (drummondiana about 2–4).

comparison_cards.caution: The single installed drummondiana habit photo cannot prove capsule seed count; do not infer it visually.

comparison_cards.title: Metziae vs ciliatiflora — raised flowering sprays
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both raise branching floral CYMES above the leaves. Metziae often bears larger white flowers and dense STALKED GLANDS on calyx and terminal branches; ciliatiflora (= old nudiflora/occidentalis source usage) often has purple flowers and sparser foliage hairs. Flower color alone is not a proof.
photo_requirements: same-scale whole terminal inflorescence and stalk origin
individual calyx with stalked gland heads in focus

comparison_cards.caution: Preserve historical R. nudiflora/R. occidentalis aliases under canonical ciliatiflora; do not duplicate these as learner species.

comparison_cards.title: Family clue — fruit hooks vs mint nutlets
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Cut open a ripe capsule and look for two valves and several hooked internal seed supports (RETINACULA). This separates typical Acanthaceae fruit from Lamiaceae's often four separate nutlets, though retinacula are NOT universal across Acanthaceae.
photo_requirements: open Ruellia mature fruit showing locules and hook supports
contrast photo of a genuine mint calyx with nutlets

visual_comparison.title: Ruellia: flower position first, hairs second, capsules last
visual_comparison.subtitle: Five physically installed exact-species photographs across three canonical species, plus one labeled offsite licensed reference for R. ciliatiflora. Existing flower portraits teach recognition and the search locations for structures; fine hairs and hooks remain targeted macro gaps.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: RAISED/BRANCHED flowering cymes → CILIATIFLORA (violet) or METZIAE (often white plus glandular calyx). NEARLY SESSILE AXILLARY flowers → HUMILIS (long visibly fringed hairs) or DRUMMONDIANA (short fine hairs and 2–4 seeds). Always verify actual hairs and fruit before a strict identification.
